newsitem.title: USA: Bonneville protests Calif. power exchange proposal.
newsitem.headline: Bonneville protests Calif. power exchange proposal.

text.p: A proposal by operators of California's planned power exchange (PX) to restrict prices paid to out-of-state suppliers is discriminatory, harmful to California customers and too complicated to implement, the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) said this week.

"The proposed rule for the PX will effectively exclude low-cost power from the pool in some hours of the year to the detriment of California consumers and California's environment," BPA said in a letter to the administrator of the California project.

The rule was included in a Monday filing to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) for final approval of the state's plan to restructure its utility industry by implementing an independent transmission system operator (ISO) and PX as of next January.
FERC is the "appropriate" venue for a final ruling on the measure, which "blatantly discrimates" against Bonneville, BPA spokesman Perry Gruber said Wednesday.

The transmission tariff rule is aimed at limiting the market power of BPA and other large sellers by preventing them from automatically receiving the California pool price during the first four years of the pool's operation.
Instead, BPA would get the highest price received by the pool in a trade of 5 MW or more between two WSCC members during that hour, or the pool price, whichever is lower.
The rule would remain in effect until BPA or other entities file an open-access tariff with FERC or demonstrate that they do not hold sway over the market.
With transmission capacity of 7,900 megawatts, BPA could dominate California's market, according to the state's three major investor owned utilities, Edison International, PG&E Corp and Enova Corp.

But Bonneville spokesman Gruber noted the federal power marketing agency does not actually own any generating resources, while the owners are separate federal agencies under separate departments of the federal government.

BPA is part of the Deparment of Energy, while the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which operates most of the Northwest hydropower projects, is within the Department of Defense, and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation is under the Interior Department.
Gruber also said the hydropower dams have evolved over the years so that power output is essentially a "residual" effect of the primary purposes of flood control and fish passage.
In addition, the regional hydroelectric system is "extremely storage deficient," he said.
"We don't have the ability to store power to sell at a time when prices are high. If anybody has market power on the West Coast it is the weather," Gruber said.

BPA also maintains that it should be able to operate under the same rules as any other power supplier, particularly since the purpose of a power exchange for the California market was to maximize consumer choice and reduce electricity prices.
